title: Combinations: a chain of forcing moves, checked to the end
outcomes: Names the links of a short combination (for example removing a defender, then a mating pattern)
Finds a two-motif sequence when told a combination exists
Plays the sequence to the last position and checks the opponent's replies
Says when an apparent combination fails at the last step

steps.text: A **combination** is a chain of forcing moves in which each move is justified by the next. It usually joins ideas you already know: a fork (*L-TAC-FORK-1*), a pin (*L-TAC-PIN-1*) or removing a defender (*L-TAC-REMOVE-DEFENDER-1*), ending in a mating pattern or a won piece. The first move may look bad. The last move pays for it.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook on c8 guards the back rank.

line.say: Qxc8+: the queen takes the rook that guards f8. This removes a defender.
Black takes the queen. Any other reply also loses to mate in two (engine).
Rf8#: nothing guards f8 now. A back-rank mate ends the chain.

claims.statement: A black piece (the rook on c8) attacks f8 at the start.
After Qxc8+ Bxc8 nothing black attacks f8.
Qxc8+ is the engine's first choice.

steps.text:
Check the whole chain, not only the first move. Play it to the last position and ask what the opponent can do there, including quiet replies and declined captures.
A combination that beats weak defence can fail against the best defence. *Rule of thumb:* if a simple move wins, play it; a complicated course adds risk.

steps.title: Play the chain to the end
steps.prompt: The first position is a combination that works. In the second, the h-pawn has moved to h6. In the third, Black's rook stands on f8. Predict, then check.
When you found a sacrifice, did you play the line to the last position before you trusted it? Which step is the easiest to skip: the last position, or the opponent's other replies?
